books.title: A therapist walks into a therapy office. But not as the therapist. As the patient. That's the premise of Lori Gottlieb's extraordinary memoir, and it's a premise that contains a radical idea within it: that the people we imagine have life figured out — the professionals, the helpers, the ones who seem to have answers — are just as lost, just as scared, just as human as the rest of us. Gottlieb is a psychotherapist in Los Angeles with a thriving practice, a popular advice column, and a TED talk that millions have watched. Then her boyfriend breaks up with her in a single phone call, and she finds herself on the other side of the couch for the first time in years, sitting across from a therapist she calls Wendell, trying to figure out how someone who spends their life helping people navigate emotional chaos can feel so thoroughly wrecked

books.title: You don't need to be a genius. That's the first thing Austin Kleon wants you to let go of — the crushing weight of the idea that only people with extraordinary talent deserve to be seen. The book itself is a kind of antidote to the cult of the lone genius, that romantic figure who toils in secret and emerges, fully formed, with a masterpiece. Kleon wrote *Show Your Work!* as a practical manifesto for everyone who's ever felt that their creative work wasn't good enough to share, or that self-promotion was somehow distasteful. The core insight is simple and freeing: instead of waiting until you've arrived, share the process of getting there. Let people see you work, think, fail, and learn. The amateur, in Kleon's framing, is not a lesser version of the professional. The amateur is someone who does something for the love of it, and who therefore has nothing to lose

books.title: Think about the last gathering you attended — a dinner party, a team meeting, a wedding, a conference. Was it memorable? Or did it blur into every other event you've ever been to, a pleasant but forgettable haze of small talk, mediocre food, and the vague sense that everyone was waiting for something to happen? Priya Parker, a conflict-resolution facilitator who has spent years designing gatherings for everyone from corporate executives to community activists, argues that the problem is not with the food, the venue, or the guest list. The problem is that most gatherings have no real purpose. They are held out of obligation, habit, or a vague desire to "connect," without any clear answer to the question that she believes should precede every gathering: why? This is the foundation of what she calls **The Art of Gathering** — the deliberate practice of designing experiences that bring people together not just to occupy the same space, but to be changed
